item.title: Is someone already using your identity? Check these 8 places
item.description: Identity theft can hide in phone accounts, medical records and utility bills long before it shows on a credit report. Eight places to check now.
item.content:encoded:
When people think about identity theft, they often start with a credit report or bank statement. Those are important places to look, but they are not the only ones. Someone using your identity may be trying to open a phone line, start utility service, use medical benefits or create a payment plan that never appears on your usual accounts.

The warning signs of identity theft can be easy to miss, especially when fraudulent activity happens outside your primary financial accounts. You do not need to investigate every record today. Start with these eight places, focusing first on accounts that could cause the most damage.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW

Review checking, savings, credit card, investment, retirement and payment-app activity for transactions you do not recognize. Look beyond purchases. A new external bank connection, authorized user, payment method, mailing address or phone number can also signal an unauthorized account change. Turn on transaction and security alerts wherever your financial institution offers them. If you find an unfamiliar transaction, contact the institution through its official website or the number on your statement. Do not use a number from a suspicious text or email.

Check all three major credit reports for accounts, hard inquiries, collections, addresses or employers you do not recognize. A fraudulent credit card, personal loan or retail-financing account may appear here even when your checking account looks normal. Use AnnualCreditReport.com to access your reports. You can currently request free online credit reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion once a week. An unfamiliar entry does not automatically mean fraud. Some lenders operate under different business names. Verify questionable information with the company before disputing it.

Pro tip: Consider freezing your credit with all three bureaus. Credit freezes are free, do not affect your credit score and can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name.

Buy now, pay later services and store-financing accounts can be easy to overlook because they may not feel like traditional credit cards. Check services you have used for unfamiliar orders, payment plans, saved addresses or account-opening messages. Some buy now, pay later loans may not appear on your traditional credit reports. Reporting practices vary by provider and loan type. Search your inbox for purchase confirmations, shipping notices and payment reminders you did not expect. Open the retailer's official app or type its web address yourself rather than clicking a link in an unexpected message.

Your phone number can provide access to other accounts because it may receive verification codes and password-reset messages. Review your carrier account for unfamiliar devices, lines, eSIMs, upgrades, address changes or changes to your account PIN. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign of a SIM swap, although outages and equipment problems can have other explanations. Contact your carrier through an official channel if the change is unexpected.

Pro tip: Ask your carrier about account PINs, port-out protection and SIM-swap security features. These safeguards may help prevent someone from transferring your number without authorization.

Review electric, gas, water, internet and other household-service accounts. Someone using your name or personal information may try to start service, change an account or leave an unpaid balance behind. Utility fraud may not appear on your credit report immediately. A bill, welcome email, service appointment or shutoff notice for an account you did not request is worth investigating. You can also request a report from the National Consumer Telecom & Utilities Exchange (NCTUE). This specialty reporting service collects information from participating phone, pay-TV and utility companies. You are entitled to one free NCTUE report every 12 months upon request. It may reveal accounts or service requests missing from your traditional credit reports, although it does not cover every provider. If you find an unfamiliar account, note the date, address and service details. Then contact the company and ask which information was used to open or change the account.

Look for explanations of benefits, medical bills, prescription notices or insurance communications related to care you did not receive. Medical identity theft can create an unexpected bill, but it can also place incorrect information in your medical record. For example, someone may use your insurance information to obtain treatment, leaving behind records that could affect future care or insurance claims. If something looks unfamiliar, contact the provider or insurer directly and ask for the records connected to the claim. Do not ignore a small bill simply because the amount seems insignificant. The inaccurate medical information may be a bigger concern.

Watch for notices from the IRS, Social Security Administration or a state benefits agency that do not match your situation. Examples include income reported by an unfamiliar employer, a tax return you did not file or unemployment benefits claimed in your name. You can review tax information through your IRS online account. You can also check your earnings history through your "my Social Security" account. If you notice unfamiliar earnings, contact the Social Security Administration about correcting your record.

Pro tip: Consider requesting an IRS Identity Protection PIN. This free, six-digit number helps prevent someone else from filing a federal tax return using your Social Security number. You can learn more at IRS.gov.

Always use official government websites to review or report suspicious activity. If an unexpected message claims to come from an agency, do not follow its links. Find the agency's website independently.

Your email and social accounts may not show a financial loss, but they can reveal whether someone is trying to take over your digital identity. Review recent sign-ins, sent messages, forwarding rules, recovery addresses, trusted devices and connected apps. Email deserves special attention because someone with access to your inbox may be able to reset passwords for other accounts. If you see unfamiliar access, change your password from a trusted device, sign out unfamiliar sessions and enable stronger multifactor authentication. Where available, use an authenticator app, passkey or security key rather than relying only on text-message verification codes.

IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT

Spread the review across four short sessions:

If nothing looks unusual, record the date of your review. The goal is to recognize unfamiliar activity, not question every legitimate bill. However, do not wait for a scheduled review if you receive a suspicious account alert or discover a potentially fraudulent transaction. Investigate those warnings immediately.

An unfamiliar message does not always mean identity theft. A lender may use a business name you do not recognize, a family member may have used a shared device or a service provider may have changed its billing name. Look for related warning signs. A new account combined with an unfamiliar address, phone change or collection notice deserves immediate attention. Even a single unauthorized transaction or account opening warrants investigation. When you are unsure, compare the record with your own statements and contact the company to explain the mismatch. Do not confirm sensitive personal details to an unexpected caller. Contact the company yourself using a verified number.

Keep the original bill, email or letter, but do not click links inside an unexpected message. Write down the date, company name, account or service involved and the first sign that something was wrong. If you call, record the department, case number and follow-up date. For credit issues, save relevant copies of all three reports. For phone, bank or email issues, keep account-change notices and screenshots. Store these records securely so you can refer to them when speaking with the company, a credit bureau or an identity theft recovery specialist.

Do not assume an unfamiliar record is fraudulent simply because you do not recognize the company name. A lender, utility provider or collection agency may use a parent-company name. Contact the organization using verified contact information. Ask for the date the account was opened, the address associated with it and the steps required to confirm whether it belongs to you. If the company confirms the account is fraudulent, ask for a fraud case number and written instructions. Then add the issue to your records and check whether related activity appears elsewhere.

Checking your accounts regularly is a smart first step, but identity theft can happen between reviews. Identity monitoring tools can help by watching for certain changes involving your personal information and alerting you when something suspicious appears.

Some services monitor credit activity, financial accounts, personal information found in data breaches and certain types of account openings. Depending on the service, you may receive alerts about unfamiliar credit inquiries, changes to your personal information or possible misuse of your identity.

Not all identity monitoring services offer the same protection. Before signing up, consider these features:

One advantage of using an identity monitoring service is having someone keeping watch for suspicious activity even when you are not actively checking your accounts. Depending on the provider and plan, these services can monitor multiple sources of information and send alerts when something needs your attention. Some also provide dedicated restoration specialists who can help guide you through the recovery process if your identity is stolen.

A paid identity monitoring service may be worth considering if you want more comprehensive monitoring and additional support when problems arise. Look for a plan that covers the types of activity most relevant to you and offers timely alerts. While no service can catch every form of identity theft, combining professional monitoring with your existing account security settings can give you an additional layer of protection. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

Pro tip: Start with the four highest-impact places: If you only have a few minutes, check your email, bank accounts, phone account and credit reports first. Those areas can help reveal whether someone is trying to access your information, move money, receive verification codes or open new credit. A clean credit report does not rule out identity theft, so return to the other four places when you have time.

YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES

I think one of the biggest mistakes people make with identity theft is assuming that a clean credit report means they're in the clear. Someone could be using your information to open a phone line, get medical care or run up a utility bill, and you might not find out until much later. I'd start by checking your email, bank accounts and wireless carrier settings. Then pull your free credit reports and take a closer look at places you might normally overlook. I'm also a big believer in freezing your credit before there's a problem. It's free, and you can temporarily lift the freeze when you need to apply for credit. Identity monitoring can provide another layer of protection, but no service can monitor everything. That's why it's important to keep an eye on your accounts, too. The sooner you spot an unfamiliar account or transaction, the sooner you can start limiting the damage.

Have you ever discovered an unfamiliar account, bill or charge that made you suspect someone was using your identity? What tipped you off? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Built from Scratch: How a rented kitchen and hand-squeezed fruit became a versatile mixer
item.description: Mixly co-founder Johnna Rossbach created a mixer for non-alcoholic drinks, dirty sodas and more through hand-squeezing fruit, funding her own project and a lot of hard work.
item.content:encoded:
Johnna Rossbach never expected to become an entrepreneur. After spending 15 years in a career that left little room for creativity, she found the motivation to build something of her own after becoming a mother.

"I wanted to show my daughters what it looks like to be empowered, and that if you’re not happy with something, change it," Rossbach said.

Rossbach loved cocktails, but she was disappointed by the mixers on store shelves. They often featured similar flavors, contained ingredients she wanted to avoid and required too much preparation.

CEO SUNDAY: AVELO AIRLINES CEO REVEALS THE HABIT HE CREDITS FOR HIS SUCCESS 

That's when she created Mixly.

Rossbach drew on her background in marketing and communications and teamed up with Megan Sather, who brought design expertise to the venture. Together, they created a line of fruit-forward cocktail mixers made with real ingredients.

The very first night the team began working on Mixly, just about everything that could go wrong did. They started at 4 p.m. and didn't finish until 3 a.m. 

When their juicer broke, they squeezed limes by hand. Then their labeler stopped working, forcing them to apply every label themselves.

Around midnight, Rossbach remembers looking at Sather and realizing they still had hours of work ahead of them. They had a choice: Call it a night and try again the following week or push through. The answer was clear. They turned up the music and kept working.

BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A FAMILY TURNED CRAFT BEER INTO A HOLIDAY TRADITION

"That was the moment we realized we made the best business partners," Rossbach said. "We had the same determination and the same willingness to roll up our sleeves and figure things out, even when nothing was going according to plan."

That night set the tone for building Mixly, which is based in New Hope, Minnesota, outside Minneapolis — and it's a big reason the co-founders have always handled their own manufacturing.

The team began developing recipes, with help from a mixologist friend to refine the flavors. Then COVID-19 disrupted their plans, forcing the founders to figure out production as they went. In an early interview, Rossbach said they were still making the products themselves in a rented kitchen while exploring ways to scale.

"When you start a business, there is no map," she said. Rossbach described the hardest part as facing the unknown: the constant decisions, self-doubt and possibility of getting things wrong.

The company has been self-funded from the beginning, without outside equity investors. The founders were intentional about building something of their own and maintaining control of the business. But that also means every dollar matters, and the stakes feel deeply personal.

"We've put our own money, time and countless hours of work into Mixly," Rossbach said.

Cocktails were the founders’ entry point, but they wanted their mixers to work for people who weren’t drinking, too. Rossbach was pregnant while the company took shape, just as the sober-curious movement began to emerge. 

The founders saw an opportunity to create a product that could be enjoyed with or without alcohol, so no one at the gathering had to feel left out.

"Let’s make this versatile. Let’s make this for everyone," Rossbach said, recalling their early thinking.

That’s why Mixly’s alcohol-free positioning isn’t a recent response to a trend. The mixers have always been alcohol-free. What has changed is the surrounding market: More consumers are looking for flavorful drinks without alcohol, and retailers are beginning to recognize the variety of occasions Mixly can serve.

CEO SUNDAY: ATOMIC WINGS CEO SHARES HIS JOURNEY FROM WALL STREET TO THE RESTAURANT BUSINESS

"I think the interest in drinking less extends well beyond January or October," Rossbach said. "People want a good option for an ordinary Tuesday, dinner with friends or a celebration."

The mixers are designed to work whether customers add a spirit or pour them over sparkling water. That calls for more than sweetness. Mixly builds flavor with fruit, acidity, herbs and bitter botanicals. Its Bitter Orange Cherry mixer, for example, uses gentian root to balance sweetness with a more complex bitter note.

"A good alcohol-free drink does not need to apologize for what is missing," Rossbach said. "It doesn’t have to imitate a cocktail to deliver that."

The founders began hearing from customers who were using Mixly in ways they hadn’t initially anticipated. One customer told them she added a mixer to her children's water for extra flavor. Others mentioned using the products in cooking and marinades.

Then Rossbach’s daughters became regulars at a local dirty soda shop. After spending about $20 on two drinks, Rossbach started thinking about how Mixly’s flavors could work in dirty sodas, too. Her daughters now make the drinks at home and have even set up a neighborhood stand.

That discovery opened a new occasion for the brand. A Mixly flavor can go into a dirty soda, a mocktail or a cocktail. The drink changes; the mixer stays the same.

In June 2026, the company changed its name from Mixly Cocktail Co. to Mixly Beverage Co. The broader name reflects products and occasions beyond the bar cart, including dirty soda and coffee.

The expansion has brought Mixly into major retailers. Five flavored syrups launched at 685 Walmart stores. The company expects its dirty soda products to reach nearly 4,000 stores by the end of November, and two holiday kits launched at 1,300 Target stores and online. Mixly says its products are now available in approximately 4,600 retail locations nationwide.

For Rossbach, that growth connects back to the idea the founders had from the beginning: Make something flavorful that people can share, whether they’re drinking alcohol or not. The market is catching up to that versatility, but it took hand-squeezed fruit, a rented kitchen and plenty of decisions without a map to get Mixly here.

When she first launched Mixly, Rossbach had an ultra-premium product line and a very specific idea of what the business would look like. But she quickly learned that what you think customers want isn't always what they actually want. The team listened, made adjustments and became more comfortable pivoting as they learned what was working and what wasn't. 

That willingness to change has helped refresh the brand, expand beyond cocktail mixers and grow into opportunities they never would have imagined when they were squeezing limes in a kitchen at 3 a.m.

item.title: Gunman opens fire from moving car in European tourist hotspot, leaving 6 dead and at least 11 wounded
item.description: A gunman, reportedly wearing military-style fatigues, allegedly opened fire from a moving vehicle on Kraków, Poland's Main Square, killing five and injuring at least 12.
item.content:encoded:
Małopolska Police confirmed a Polish gunman opened fire at a popular tourist destination in Kraków on Saturday, killing six people and wounding at least eleven more.

Of the six dead, four are women and two are men, according to Małopolska Police. 

Shooting from a moving vehicle, the gunman allegedly targeted people at random, injuring civilians as well as police during the attack on Kraków's bustling Main Square.

Video posted on social media showed people running while gunshots rang out.

Police shot and wounded the suspect during a gunfight and the area is now secured, according to authorities.

TEEN WEARING HELMET CAMERA KILLS WORKER AT POLISH SCHOOL AMID FEARS OF COPYCAT ATTACKS

The suspect, who has only been identified by police as a "citizen of the Republic of Poland," was wearing military-style fatigues and used a military-style rifle to carry out the attack, Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Kraków police, told Polish network TVN24.

Authorities also found numerous other weapons and ammunition in the suspect's car, Cisło said.

GUNMAN KILLS 6 AT YOUTH WELFARE FACILITY IN SUSPECTED CHILD CUSTODY DISPUTE: REPORTS

Małopolska Police released a statement Saturday afternoon denying reports that a police officer died and that another perpetrator is being sought.

"The only known perpetrator of the incident is in police custody," officials said.

A public train driver reported around 3 p.m. local time that his vehicle had been shot by a man in a moving car, shattering his window.

GUNFIRE SHATTERS TORONTO LATIN STREET FESTIVAL, LEAVING AT LEAST 2 DEAD AND MULTIPLE WOUNDED

Police vehicles, ambulances, and a Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter surrounded the scene at Main Square, which is located in the country's second-largest city.

Polish Police said in a statement on X, "in connection with the tragic incident that occurred in Kraków, National Police Commander Inspector General Marek Boroń is heading to the scene."

Polish leaders reacted to the scene in a series of public statements on social media.

'NOT ON OUR WATCH': GLOBAL LAW ENFORCEMENT LEADERS UNITE IN POLAND AGAINST HATE

"My deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims of the tragic attack in Kraków. My highest praise for the heroic police officers who risked their lives. And a heartfelt appeal to politicians of all stripes: do not exploit this tragedy. We will establish all the circumstances of this crime," Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote in a statement posted to X.

Tusk also assured the public that police are investigating the background and details of the attack.

POLISH PRESIDENT TURNS PLANE AROUND AFTER 'COUP' AT NATION’S TOP COURT

Poland's president Karol Nawrocki also weighed in.

"I am deeply concerned by reports of the tragic events in central Kraków. My thoughts are with the victims, those injured and their families. I remain in contact with the relevant services and expect a full explanation of the circumstances surrounding these tragic events," he wrote on X.

HUNGARY AND POLAND DEFEND TOUGH MIGRATION POLICIES AS FRANCE REELS FROM VIOLENT UNREST

Nawrocki also revealed that the head of Poland's National Security Bureau is on his way to the city to investigate.

The United States Ambassador to Poland, Tom Rose, shared sympathies in a post on X.

"We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Kraków, a savage and murderous attack that’s shattered the peace of Poland," Rose wrote. "America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Kraków."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the shooting as "shocking," in a statement on X, also extending condolences to the victims' loved ones.

"There can be no justification for this attack, and we trust the perpetrator will face justice," Zelenskyy wrote. "We wish strength and a speedy recovery to the injured and to everyone affected by this tragedy. Ukraine stands in solidarity with Poland and the Polish people. People have the right to safety."

Shootings are exceedingly rare in Poland, a country that ranks among the world's lowest in gun-related deaths at 0.2 to 0.4 deaths per 100,000 residents, according to a study conducted by Medical University of Gdansk researchers.

The shooting comes amidst a constitutional crisis in Poland, pitting Tusk's pro-European Union government and the national conservative opposition.

Nawrocki's election to the presidency from the opposition has tumbled the nation's Parliament into a deadlock, seeing the executive use his veto power to block the appointments of would-be tribunal leaders, resulting in a paralyzed Constitutional Tribunal 

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Big Ten coach who had an abysmal record in the SEC thinks his team would be ranked in the SEC
item.description: Bret Bielema claims his 6-3 Illinois squad would be a top-15 team in the SEC, but his 11-29 record at Arkansas tells a very different story.
item.content:encoded:
Illinois head football coach Bret Bielema, who went 11-29 against the SEC during his five-year run at Arkansas, thinks his current program would be ranked ... If it were in the SEC.

Quite the spin!

TIM BRANDO JOINS DAN DAKICH ON 'DON'T @ ME' TO DISCUSS INDIANA COACH CURT CIGNETTI'S CFP 'BIAS' COMMENTS

Now, to be fair, Illinois is having a decent season. The Fighting Illini are coming off a 24-13 win over Nebraska Friday night, and sit at 6-3 as the regular season begins its final month. It's been a good year for Illinois up to this point. Credit where it's due, Bielema has the fellas playing well in 2026.

For some reason, though, the SEC continues to be on the brains of every Big Ten coach in America right now. Earlier this week, Curt Cignetti took a shot at the conference after the initial CFP rankings was overloaded with SEC teams.

BRET BIELEMA ROASTS NICK SABAN, SEC, AT BIG TEN MEDIA DAYS: 'THEY WANT TO LIVE IN 2005 FOREVER'

After last night's win, Bielema joined the chorus, saying his unranked Fighting Illini would be in the mix if they played in the SEC.

Take a look:

"But to be in this job, where we’re at right now, 6-3, we beat another 5-3 team. If we were in the SEC, we’d probably be a top-15 team."

Thoughts? First impressions?

So, Bielema is correct in the fact that if Illinois was currently 6-3 and played an SEC conference schedule, it would be ranked. Not sure it would be a top-15 team, but certainly ranked. I guess it depends who the wins/losses came against.

But also, if Illinois played in the SEC ... I'm not sure the Fighting Illini would be a 6-3 team right now. Their current wins have come against:

One ranked win probably doesn't cut it. Now, Illinois' three losses? Purdue, Duke, and Ohio State (42-19). It doesn't feel like an "SEC schedule," at least not this season. The wins aren't impressive, beyond beating an Oregon team that has no business being ranked with Dante Moore out.

As for Bielema's actual record in the conference he can't get off his brain ...

He went 11-29 against the SEC over four years at Arkansas, including 0-8 in his first season. Not saying that was completely his fault because that roster certainly wasn't his, but the numbers are still the numbers.

And the numbers say Bret Bielema's current team would be nowhere close to 6-3 in the SEC right now.

It's a down year for the Big Ten. Let's just be honest for a second.

That conference has dominated this sport for a few years now, but it's just a down year. It happens. Ohio State lost its starting QB. Oregon did, too. Penn State stinks. Michigan stinks.

Indiana is currently ranked fourth, but needed overtime to beat both Michigan AND Minnesota.

Everyone wants to complain about the committee showing "SEC bias" in the initial batch of rankings earlier this week. That's fine. That's fair.

But the options weren't great.

item.title: Son sounds alarm after father's medically assisted death in Canada: Way past appropriate'
item.description: Eric Edmeades says Canada's MAiD program moved so fast his father died before the family could prepare, warning safeguards have gone too far.
item.content:encoded:
A Canadian man's decision to end his life through the country's medically assisted dying program left his son stunned by how quickly the process unfolded, and now he's warning that the system has gone "way past appropriate."

Eric Edmeades, founder of Speaker Nation, a training platform for speakers that teaches presentation skills and more, told Fox News Digital this week that his father Baz, who was in his late 70s and struggling with a combination of medical problems, began discussing Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) program after his health deteriorated in late 2023.

But what Edmeades expected to be a months-long process suddenly accelerated, leaving the family with little time to prepare.

I'M 25 WITH A TERMINAL DISEASE. WE NEED AN FDA COMMISSIONER THAT HEARS PEOPLE LIKE ME

Edmeades said the family started taking the issue seriously in January, but at that stage, projections were that it would take at least six months. He and his wife traveled to Vancouver at the beginning of 2024 to visit his father. At that stage, it was still a speculative thing that was months away.

"And then all of a sudden it was like, ‘No, it's next week,’" Edmeades recalled.

His father died via MAiD on Feb. 27, 2024.

He had been experiencing a sharp decline in his physical health and independence, particularly during the COVID-era lockdowns, according to his son.

"He had been incredibly healthy most of his life," Edmeades said, describing a combination of symptoms that included epilepsy and neurological pain.

Edmeades also questioned whether interactions between his father's medications could have contributed to his deteriorating condition.

"When the lockdowns came along, and he could no longer go out and walk all the time, it really had a marked decrease in his physical ability and his sense of freedom and all that kind of stuff," he said.

"And then there just came this point where life started sounding pointless to him," Edmeades said.

CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH

Edmeades said his father had previously spoken about suicide, making his initial interest in medically assisted dying less surprising to the family.

"Given that it wasn't the first time that he talked about suicide in his life, it wasn't particularly shocking, but he also wasn't talking about it in really alarmist terms. So, I wasn't overly worried about it," he said.

Edmeades and his wife had already planned a trip to Vancouver and were able to spend time with his father before his death.

"And one of the things I'm incredibly grateful for is that I had incidentally booked a trip out to Vancouver, and my wife and I got to spend time with him," Edmeades recalled.

He thought he and and his wife would have another opportunity to visit.

NEW YORK NUNS' CHALLENGE TO ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW IS ABOUT PROTECTING FREEDOM, LAWYER SAYS

Edmeades said he was not in contact with his father's medical providers at the time and did not fully understand what had happened until afterward.

"It happened so quickly that I only really started to piece together what happened when it was done," he said.

Other family members and friends had also expressed concerns about his father's decision, according to Edmeades. He recalled that his brother openly opposed the decision and that one of his father's close friends spent approximately 45 minutes discussing the matter with him during his final days.

"At that stage, you know, for him, the decision was made," Edmeades said.

The experience has left Edmeades questioning whether Canada's assisted-dying program has adequate safeguards.

He acknowledged that there may be circumstances in which medically assisted dying is appropriate but argued that Canada's implementation has gone too far.

"What I see happening in Canada is way past appropriate," he said.

Edmeades also raised concerns about the government's role in overseeing the system, arguing that decisions about eligibility should be insulated from political influence and potential financial incentives.

"If I had to press a button and decide whether the MAiD program existed or didn't exist, I would say this," Edmeades said. "It should only ever exist if, and I mean if the process for approving people, it would be completely independent of government, and there could be no benefit to those people in making that preference in making that decision. Because otherwise there's a slippery slope, and we see that slippery slope."

According to the Government of Canada, individuals seeking medical assistance in dying (MAiD) must be at least 18 years old, capable of making their own medical decisions, and eligible for publicly funded healthcare. They must also voluntarily request the procedure without outside pressure and provide informed consent. To qualify, applicants must have a serious, incurable illness, disease or disability, be experiencing an advanced and irreversible decline in their abilities, and face persistent physical or psychological suffering they consider intolerable and that cannot be relieved in a way they find acceptable.

The government also announced legislation on Oct. 27, 2026, that would allow advance requests while preventing the planned expansion of MAiD eligibility to people whose sole underlying medical condition is mental illness.

According to the BBC, Canada’s MAiD law, which legalized euthanasia in 2016, is responsible for one in every 20 deaths in Canada.

NEW YORK NUNS WILL NOT BE FORCED TO COMPLY WITH ASSISTED-SUICIDE LAW WHILE CASE PROGRESSES

A report from the Canadian Medical Association Journal covered by EWTN News claimed that implementing assisted suicide will "save" the Canadian healthcare system between $34.7 and $136.8 million per year. The study noted that patients and physicians should not consider costs when making such grave decisions.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Ian McLeod, senior advisor for media relations and Conseiller principal for the Department of Justice Canada, said, "Canadian law is extremely clear: medical assistance in dying (MAID) requires a voluntary request, freedom from external pressure, and the person’s informed consent, among other stringent eligibility criteria and safeguards. Knowingly failing to comply with these eligibility criteria and safeguards is a criminal offence."

McLeod continued, "In the current MAID structure found in Canada’s Criminal Code, the mental illness exclusion is meant to exclude eligibility for MAID on the basis of a mental illness, including suicidal ideation. The proposed amendment to the mental illness exclusion in Bill C-41, the proposed Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act, which was introduced on October 27, 2026, is meant to reinforce this."

McLeod added, "This is why the Bill reinforces that, in situations where a person has a mental illness and an eligible medical condition (e.g. physical or neurodegenerative illness), eligibility must be determined on the basis of the qualifying medical condition. A mental illness may contribute to a person’s suffering, but it cannot be the basis for determining that the MAID eligibility criteria are met. Importantly, having a mental illness does not, in itself, make a person ineligible for MAID."

McLeod said that patients whose natural deaths are not reasonably foreseeable must undergo eligibility assessments by two independent doctors or nurse practitioners, with at least 90 full days between the start of the first assessment and the assisted death.

That waiting period, according to McLeod, can be shortened if both assessments are complete, both practitioners agree the patient is at imminent risk of losing the ability to consent, and the practitioner providing MAiD determines that a shorter period is appropriate.

McLeod emphasized that federal requirements establish minimum safeguards, while provinces and territories oversee how MAiD is administered and may impose additional protections. He said questions about the program's oversight and delivery should therefore be directed to provincial or territorial authorities.

item.title: Relationship expert explains why people ghost and what they may regret later
item.description: Relationship expert Monica Ricci shares why ghosting is a classic avoidance behavior and what it truly says about the person who disappears.
item.content:encoded:
If you've ever dated someone who stopped reaching out and responding to texts, without any conversation about ending the relationship, you’ve been ghosted.

"Ghosting," or the sudden absence or unresponsiveness of a potential partner, is more than just feeling ignored by someone you’re interested in, according to Monica Ricci, a Georgia-based relationship coach — it's a complete disappearance without closure.

Why do people ghost? Ricci suggested it’s a "classic avoidance behavior." 

"It's the same reason we procrastinate — we're avoiding some kind of discomfort," she said.

THE MARRIAGE WARNING SIGN THAT MAY BE WORSE THAN FIGHTING — AND 4 WAYS TO TURN THINGS AROUND

"It could be a fear of having a really hard conversation. It could be not wanting to disappoint a person," Ricci went on. "Someone could ghost because they just don't care enough. They're just not invested enough that they believe it [would] warrant communicating to say, ‘Hey, this isn't working for me.'"

Those who do the ghosting may feel a sudden sense of relief, according to Ricci, but may also have lingering guilt around how the relationship was left unfinished.

A new paper based on three studies, published in Sage Journals, suggests people who are ghosted underestimate the guilt and remorse felt by those who cut off contact.

5 MARRIAGE MISTAKES COUPLES MAKE WITHOUT REALIZING IT — AND HOW TO AVOID THEM

"There's a part of you that may know that wasn't the best way to handle it," Ricci said. "And so it may stay with you a lot longer because it calls into question the kind of person you want to be."

It’s easy to take ghosting personally, she noted.

"But the truth is, if you're being ghosted, it says more about the person who ghosted you and their ability to have honest communication, their ability to step up in an uncomfortable situation and really choose their behavior over their discomfort."

After a ghosting, the brain will automatically begin searching for patterns and answers to "make things make sense," Ricci said.

WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY — PLUS THE ‘RED FLAG’ TO AVOID

At some point, moving forward means accepting that you may never get an explanation and recognizing that being ghosted is not a reflection of your worth, according to the expert.

"If a person can't have a conversation with you at the beginning of a relationship that is honest and frank, they probably weren't your person anyway," she added.

Ricci, whose expertise is based on the Gottman Method — an approach to couples therapy focused on building emotional intimacy, improving communication and managing conflict — said seemingly difficult conversations can be easier than people expect.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"When you want to communicate that this dating relationship is not a good fit anymore, it's easiest to be very direct and brief," she said.

This can be as simple as sending a text saying, "I have enjoyed getting to know you. I'm not feeling the kind of connection that I need to move forward, and I wish you all the best in finding a great match."

"You're honest, you're truthful, you're not making it about them being a bad person," she said. "You're saying, ‘I'm just not feeling the kind of connection I need to move forward.'"

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Although being forthright is the respectful option, it's not possible to control how the other person will feel or react, Ricci noted.

"And this is sometimes where the ghosting comes from – we don't want to make someone feel bad," she said. "It’s this illusion that we have some control over how a person feels … But the reality is the least painful and kindest option is to just be direct."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

However, in a situation where you are being harassed, stalked or abused, ghosting may be the safest option, Ricci emphasized.

"If someone is treating you really poorly, or harassing you, or stalking you … ghosting is absolutely the most appropriate," she said. "Cutting a person off completely, not responding, is the safest, smartest way to go."

item.title: Defense attorney in Tupac Shakur murder trial found dead at 55: report
item.description: Michael Sanft, the Las Vegas attorney who defended Duane Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder trial, was reportedly found dead days after filing an appeal in the case.
item.content:encoded:
Michael Sanft, the Las Vegas defense attorney who represented Duane "Keffe D" Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder case, was found dead inside his home Friday morning, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal. He was 55.

The cause and manner of Sanft's death has not yet been determined. Police told the Las Vegas outlet that the death did not appear suspicious.

Michael Sloan, a close friend who rode motorcycles with Sanft, according to the report, confirmed his death and remembered the attorney as a devoted friend.

DUANE 'KEFFE D' DAVIS FOUND GUILTY OF FIRST-DEGREE MURDER IN 1996 KILLING OF TUPAC SHAKUR

"He was one of my best friends and one of the best human beings I knew," Sloan shared

Fox News Digital reached out to the Clark County coroner's office and the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department for comment.

TUPAC SHAKUR MURDER TRIAL'S FIRST WEEK SEES HEATED TESTIMONY FROM RELUCTANT WITNESSES WITH OLD GANGLAND TIES

Sanft's death comes after a courtroom battle that ended with Davis, 63, becoming the first person convicted in connection with Shakur's 1996 murder.

A Nevada jury found Davis guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon in August. He was sentenced Oct. 13 to 40 years to life behind bars, according to The Associated Press.

The verdict marked a significant development in a case that has drawn international attention for nearly three decades.

Shakur was riding in a BMW with Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight near the Las Vegas Strip on Sept. 7, 1996, when a gunman in a white Cadillac opened fire.

Knight survived with minor injuries. Shakur, one of hip-hop's biggest stars at the time, died six days later at age 25.

Prosecutors argued Davis orchestrated the killing after his nephew was involved in a fight with Shakur and Knight earlier that night.

During closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal told jurors Davis obtained a gun and "went hunting" for the two men. Prosecutors also pointed to Davis' own statements placing himself inside the Cadillac used in the shooting.

Sanft disputed the prosecution's case, telling jurors there was no evidence beyond Davis' statements placing his client in Las Vegas or inside the Cadillac.

Jurors deliberated for about three hours before finding Davis guilty.

The decision prompted an emotional scene in court, with Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur, crying as the verdict was read. Davis' son covered his face with one hand.

The jury consisted of 12 jurors and four alternates. The panel heard testimony over nine days from 24 prosecution witnesses and three defense witnesses.

Davis was held without bail after the verdict and before his sentencing in October.

No further details about Sanft’s death were immediately available.

item.title: Ravens tell teams Derrick Henry staying put amid NFL trade deadline rumors: report
item.description: Derrick Henry is not available for trade before the NFL deadline, per reports, as the Baltimore Ravens try to salvage a season amid injury woes.
item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Ravens’ playoff hopes are teetering amid quarterback injury issues and a four-game losing streak, which includes a 33-10 rout by the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday night.

While Baltimore did trade for Jacoby Brissett to hopefully put an end to their signal-caller woes, rumors have begun swirling around one of the team’s stars: running back Derrick Henry.

The NFL trade deadline is on Tuesday, and some were of the belief the Ravens would at least listen to trade offers for the 32-year-old veteran back – a team that could be one piece like Henry away from a complete squad ready for a Super Bowl run.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But the Ravens think otherwise, telling teams that Henry is not available before the Nov. 10 deadline, per ESPN.

The speculation surrounded two of Henry’s former head coaches, with John Harbaugh and the New York Giants reportedly in the aggressive buying stage, and running back is where they seem to be looking. The Giants are among those very interested in Jonathan Taylor with the Indianapolis Colts.

New England Patriots’ Mike Vrabel could’ve also been a good spot for a Henry reunion, especially given that TreVeyon Henderson was just hospitalized after suffering "unexplainable" neurological symptoms.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Henry is a key cog in making this Declan Doyle-led offense work for the Ravens, but it hasn’t looked that way among recent quarterback injuries, most notably to two-time MVP Lamar Jackson.

Jackson dealt with a high-ankle sprain before a much-needed return last week against the Buffalo Bills. However, on his first snap of the game, his throwing hand collided with Bills pass rusher Greg Rousseau’s hand. He was placed on the injured reserved after needing surgery to repair his thumb.

So, Tyler "Snoop" Huntley had to resume his role as the team’s starter, doing so in the games Jackson missed earlier in the season. But Huntley suffered a turf toe injury in the same Bills matchup, knocking him out for the remainder of the season.

That led to emergency quarterback Joe Fagnano, a rookie out of UConn, taking over in a 36-10 loss to the Bills. The Ravens made the move to trade for Brissett after the Arizona Cardinals benched him in the second half of a comeback win over the Dallas Cowboys in Week 8, where head coach Mike LaFleur gave the reins to Gardner Minshew, and later named rookie Carson Beck his backup entering Week 9.

But Brissett’s arrival in Baltimore wasn’t going to come before "Thursday Night Football" against a very good Jaguars team. With steady rain coming down, the Ravens’ offense couldn’t get anything going with Fagnano under center, and now the team hopes Brissett can keep them competitive enough to battle for a playoff spot.

There is still a chance Jackson will be returning post-thumb surgery, but he’s forced to miss the next four games on the IR. At 4-5, the Ravens needed Brissett to hold down the fort at least, with Baltimore losing by at least 20 points in their last three games.

All of this to say, the Ravens need a running threat like Henry if they wish to salvage the season that is starting to slip away.

"I have not mentioned me going anywhere else," a frustrated Henry said following the loss. "I’m saying, ‘Let’s go back to work. Let’s try to get better and turn this thing around.’"

item.title: Tennis star Sorana Cirstea immediately retires from the sport after upset loss at Hong Kong Open
item.description: Sorana Cirstea stunned the tennis world by retiring after her Hong Kong Open quarterfinal loss to Alexandra Shubladze despite a career-high ranking.
item.content:encoded:
You know when something goes wrong at work and you just want to slam your laptop shut, walk out of the office and quit? Apparently, professional athletes know that feeling, too.

Tennis star Sorana Cirstea lost 6-2, 6-3 to Alexandra Shubladze in the quarterfinals of the Hong Kong Open on Friday night and shocked the tennis world by retiring from the sport immediately after the match.

Cirstea, 36, was the No. 1 seed at the Hong Kong Open and the 15th-ranked player in the world. She came into the season saying 2026 would be her final year on tour and decided to follow through with that plan after the upset loss.

"I was running on empty, I had no energy left. It's been a long year. I need to step back and process all of this before making a final announcement, which should come in a few weeks."

Unlike many people who rage-quit their jobs because they are fed up, Cirstea was thriving. Her No. 15 ranking was the highest of her career.

Cirstea became just the fourth woman age 36 or older to finish a season ranked among the world's top 16 in the last 40 years, joining Martina Navratilova, Serena Williams and Venus Williams.

In May, Cirstea defeated then-No. 1-ranked Aryna Sabalenka at the Italian Open and was already receiving pleas from fans to keep playing.

"Everyone has been asking me, like, ‘You cannot retire, you cannot retire!’" Cirstea said in May at the Italian Open, according to the New York Post.

During her career, the Romanian tennis player has won four singles titles and earned more than $13 million in prize money, according to the Women's Tennis Association (WTA) website.

item.title: Martha Stewart begs America for forgiveness after 'stupid' homeless Halloween costume sparks backlash
item.description: Martha Stewart admits her homeless Halloween costume was "stupid" after her grandson warned her it was "tone-deaf" before the backlash began.
item.content:encoded:
Martha Stewart is asking Americans for forgiveness after her Halloween costume drew harsh criticism.

The lifestyle mogul, 85, admitted her decision to dress as a person experiencing homelessness was "stupid," and revealed that her grandson had warned her about the outfit before the public criticism began.

"According to my grandson, I was tone-deaf," Stewart said while explaining how the controversial costume came together during a Friday appearance on the "Today" show.

MARTHA STEWART ADDRESSES BACKLASH AFTER DRESSING AS HOMELESS PERSON FOR HALLOWEEN

Stewart's Halloween costume featured ripped jeans, a distressed shirt and a cardboard sign reading "I AM HUNGRY. HELP ME!!"

During a discussion about lessons learned on the morning show, she acknowledged that she needed to be more mindful and "pay closer attention to social issues. Be aware."

The businesswoman said she cares deeply about the challenges facing Americans but acknowledged that her costume was a mishap.

"But I made a mistake. I mean, I was stupid. Yeah. What else can I say? What else can I say? I'm so sorry," Stewart said.

MARTHA STEWART GETS CANDID ABOUT PLASTIC SURGERY, DATING AS SHE TURNS 85

She also asked her fans and the public to forgive her, saying, "I hope that my followers and my fans and the rest of America forgives me for doing something that was not meant in any way to be a bad thing."

The longtime television personality said she put together the costume at the last minute after initially deciding not to dress up for Halloween.

A chocolate stain on her white sweater also helped inspire the last-minute costume, Stewart said. She joked that "Today" co-anchor Craig Melvin was responsible for the stain before clarifying that she was only kidding.

In her initial statement to Page Six, Stewart said the costume was not meant to mock people experiencing homelessness.

"I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention," she said.

item.title: DEPROGRAMMED: She entered Columbia a liberal. A fight over English lit turned her conservative
item.description: A Columbia University graduate says speech suppression and grading bias in English classes pushed her from liberalism to the conservative movement.
item.content:encoded:
The sharp flick of textbook pages, the smell of studied parchment and a litany of knowledge surrounded Liza Libes during her time at Columbia University, an experience she entered as a bright-eyed, liberal freshman, before leaving a conservative with a deep commitment to free speech.

"I was very upset with my suppression of speech. You know, I'm a writer. The biggest thing to me is the ability to be able to say what you think, to write what you think. And I wasn't able to write exactly what I thought in my English classrooms," Libes told Fox News Digital.

"I would get Cs when I would argue in favor of the patriarchy. And then when I argued that, you know, so-and-so was subverting gender norms, then I would get an A… It was just this kind of gradual accumulation," she continued.

OKLAHOMA STUDENT FLUNKED BY TA AFTER TOUTING CHRISTIAN BELIEFS IN GENDER ESSAY, DIRECTS OTHERS TO ‘PUSH BACK’

Libes detailed an experience she had during an English class involving an assignment about Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream," in which her professor said the play centered on "queer desire."

Libes, the founder of the Substack "Pens & Poison," disagreed.

"I just wrote about the play, I didn't touch on queer desire. She took off a couple points from my exam because I didn't mention queer desire in the class for the midterm. So I thought that was a very bizarre thing for her to do," she said.

"There [were] a couple other professors [that] I really disagreed with in terms of the way that they were teaching literature, the way they were kind of creating this Marxist ideology from a lot of literary works and kind of thrusting the Marxist teachings on so many great works of literature," Libes continued.

LIBERAL FACULTY STILL HUGELY OUTNUMBER CONSERVATIVES IN HIGHER EDUCATION: REPORT

"I felt very stifled as a writer and I think that that was kind of my last straw," Libes added.

"I wanted to be in a place where I could just… express my values, express my beliefs in writing and also in conversation… By the time I was a senior, I very much identified with the conservative movement," she continued.

Libes received a master's degree in English and comparative literature in 2020, after earning her bachelor's degree in English literature in 2019.

When asked about the campus environment beyond the classroom, Libes described an underlying "expectation" to hold "certain viewpoints," saying she knew she was going to be "socially ostracized in some way."

FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS

Libes grew up in what she called a "post-Soviet household," speaking Russian with her immigrant parents and grandmother.

"One of the things that was very big in my household was just this idea of freedom, right, because my parents had come from the Soviet Union, there was a lot of oppression there," she said.

"Obviously, we did not like socialism because socialism was one of the ways that a lot of this oppression was perpetrated. And I thought of myself always as a liberal because I stood for freedom. I was against oppression, I was, you know, pro-free speech — those to me were very liberal ideas, those were the ideas that I grew up with in my household," Libes continued.

30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS

"When I got to Columbia, I very quickly realized that those ideas were no longer part of the left, that the left liked to suppress speech, the left liked to ostracize anyone who didn't hold, you know, certain opinions or beliefs," she added.

Libes encourages other young people to stand by what they believe.

"Don't be afraid [of] expressing your beliefs and don't let, kind of, peer pressure or other people sway you into believing one thing or another," Libes said.

Columbia University did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

item.title: Live WWII-era grenades turn up in unlikely place as bomb squad warns of danger
item.description: Five live World War II grenades were confirmed to be still active by the Austin, Texas, bomb squad after a former FBI buyer found them in estate sale boxes.
item.content:encoded:
A resident of Austin, Texas, recently found five live World War II-era grenades inside boxes purchased at an estate sale — prompting an urgent police response.

The unusual discovery was announced by the Austin Police Association (APA), which represents Austin police officers, earlier in October.

In an Instagram post, the APA said the resident purchased several boxes at the estate sale and discovered what appeared to be WWII-era grenades while going through them.

MYSTERY SURROUNDS GERMAN SOLDIERS FOUND NEAR MUD-COVERED WWII MOTORCYCLE IN DANUBE

"APD's Bomb Squad confirmed they were live and active," the post said.

Austin Police Department (APD) officers secured the scene and established a perimeter to protect nearby residents while awaiting explosives specialists, according to the association.

The bomb squad recovered five grenades, according to Sgt. Issa Kafena, the supervisor of the APD Bomb Squad.

Kafena told Fox News Digital that, though officers could not determine exactly when the grenades were manufactured, they appeared to be about 80 years old.

TEXAS ROAD CONSTRUCTION UNEARTHS 'COLOSSAL' PREHISTORIC REMAINS OF 'BIG OL' ANIMALS'

The buyer seemed to recognize the potential danger and contacted authorities.

"I believe the person was former FBI, so [they] immediately kind of took precautions to make sure everything was safe, called 911, and patrol responded and then immediately called us," he said.

Despite their age, Kafena — who did not personally respond to the incident — warned that the grenades still posed a danger.

RARE CANNONBALL EMERGES FROM GROUND AT THE ALAMO, LIKELY UNTOUCHED FOR NEARLY 190 YEARS

"All ordnance ... there's an inherent danger to any and all of it, especially if it's military ordnance," Kafena said. 

"It's designed to hurt and kill people."

He added that the grenades could have injured someone had they functioned as designed.

Though the APA described the incident as an "unusual call," Kofina said discoveries of old military explosives are not entirely unheard of by authorities.

"It's more common than you think," Kafena said.

The officer said the bomb squad handles over 400 deployments annually, including approximately 150 to 175 call-outs, many of which involve discovered military ordnance or equipment.

"In this region, we cover 8,400 square miles in the 10-county capital area of government's region," he said. "And we go all over the central Texas area for calls like this fairly frequently."

Once the grenades were recovered, bomb squad officers safely disposed of and destroyed them, Kafena said.

Above all, Kafena urged anyone who discovers old military explosives to leave them undisturbed and contact authorities immediately.

"If you ever find it, don't touch it, call 911 immediately and have the bomb squad come out and help address the situation," he said.

The Austin discovery is not the only recent case of military ordnance turning up in unexpected places.

Last fall, a father and son unexpectedly discovered more than 150 World War II-era artillery shells while metal detecting in a Czech forest, prompting a two-day bomb squad operation.

item.title: MARK PENN: The midterms revealed a nation of unhappy capitalists. Here's the cure
item.description: A Fox News poll shows capitalism holds a 23-point favorability edge over socialism, yet 75% of voters say the economy is not so good or poor.
item.content:encoded:
America is suffering from having too many unhappy capitalists.

Indeed, in the Fox News poll of voters, 75% said the economy was not so good or poor. And 44% said their economic conditions were deteriorating rather than improving.

America is a nation obsessed with and reeling from increases in the cost of living. It is a bit odd because inflation has come down from 9% a year under President Biden to about 3% a year under President Trump, while economic growth and employment are excellent by any normal standard. We even have the lowest poverty rate in American history. And yet people are unhappy, and on Tuesday they voted for the people who were responsible for the lion’s share of inflation and who spent 10 years and $2 trillion on measures designed to increase the cost of gasoline and other fossil fuels.

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

And they also elected six new members of the Democratic Socialists of America to Congress this week, bringing their total to at least eight members advancing radical economic redistribution.

But when socialism was directly on the ballot on November 3, it failed. The California wealth tax, which would start a new era of taxation on wealth — a direct confiscation of property — went down in flames, with 57% or more rejecting it.

RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY

And in that same Fox News poll, 56% of respondents viewed capitalism favorably and 32% unfavorably. For socialism, 33% viewed it favorably and 53% unfavorably; the rest didn’t know enough to say.

So, capitalism had a 23-point net advantage in favorability. When asked in another Fox News poll whether moving the U.S. away from capitalism toward socialism would be good or bad, 38% said good and 61% said bad.

LEE CARTER: SOCIALISM MEANS TWO WILDLY DIFFERENT THINGS TO REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS

And interestingly, in a recent Harris poll, young people at first said they were for socialism but then said they wanted to own their own businesses and homes and be paid not equally, but according to their merits.

SOCIALISM'S GROWING APPEAL MEETS AN AWKWARD REALITY CHECK ON COLLEGE CAMPUS

So deep down, most of these socialists are really just capitalists drafted into a movement they know little about, fed by a stream of TikTok videos. Indeed, the social media platform itself is a form of capitalism, with people paid according to their clicks. Imagine the uproar if we declared tomorrow that all TikTok creators would make the same amount and that we were confiscating 5% per year of the followers of influencers with over 1 million followers. That would be the end of social media as we know it, given the uproar.

So maybe socialism is in vogue, and some socialist candidates are slipping into Congress. But make no mistake, they are getting beaten when their proposals are isolated and put on the ballot. Capitalism still trumps socialism, and if you call it free enterprise, it soars another 15 points.

So what we really have right now is a lot of unhappy capitalists who see themselves as having trouble buying a home, a car or other ingredients of middle-class life. The numbers suggest otherwise, but there is no arguing with their belief that the economy is not on their side. But the real fix to these problems lies in policies far simpler than socialism — lower interest rates, lower taxes, more U.S. energy production and affordable health care without a big government takeover.

item.title: 11-night Caribbean cruise abruptly canceled after Coast Guard detains ship
item.description: After the U.S. Coast Guard identified significant deficiencies, the MSC Poesia was detained in Miami, stranding over 2,000 cruise passengers. An attorney weighed in.
item.content:encoded:
A major cruise line abruptly canceled an 11-night voyage to the Caribbean this week when the U.S. Coast Guard detained its ship in Miami.

The Coast Guard announced on Nov. 3 that MSC Poesia had been detained due to deficiencies with systems aboard the ship.

"The Coast Guard cannot currently comment on the specifics of an ongoing Port State Control Examination, but we have identified deficiencies with systems on board the vessel that we are addressing with MSC," said Capt. Frank Florio, commander, U.S. Coast Guard Sector Miami, in a press release issued by the Coast Guard.

OUTRAGED CRUISE PASSENGERS BLAST COMPANY'S 'IDIOTIC' NEW DRESS CODE CRACKDOWN

The MSC Poesia will remain detained at the Miami port until the deficiencies are fixed and the ship is cleared to depart, the release added.

"We have made the difficult decision to cancel the current sailing," an MSC Cruises spokesperson told Fox News Digital about the situation. "We recognize how disappointing and frustrating this news is for our guests, and we sincerely apologize for the disruption to their holiday."

"Prior to departure, a regulatory matter arose that required resolution. Despite our efforts to address the matter, we were unable to resolve it in time for the sailing to proceed," the spokesperson added.

"Guests will receive a full refund of their cruise fare, and we are providing support to assist with their journey home."

CRUISE TIPPING CHARGES ARE 'OUT OF CONTROL.' SAY PASSENGERS AS COMPANIES TOUT 'EXCEPTIONAL SERVICE'

The Coast Guard said its Port State Control program inspects foreign-flagged commercial vessels calling at U.S. ports to ensure they meet applicable safety, security and environmental standards.

"When substantial noncompliance is identified, the Coast Guard may detain a vessel until the deficiencies that prevent its departure are corrected," the release said.

More than 2,000 people were aboard when the ship was detained, according to the blog "Cruise Critic."

The MSC Poesia was scheduled to leave Miami on Nov. 1 and return Nov. 12, with stops in Jamaica, Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica, Honduras and Belize, according to CruiseMapper.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Alex Perez, a maritime attorney at the Miami law firm Lipcon, Margulies & Winkleman, told Fox News Digital it's very rare for a cruise ship carrying thousands of people to be detained rather than cited.

Cruise ships in U.S. ports are inspected frequently, Perez said.

But "the fact that this cruise ship was detained with passengers on board when [it was] about to embark on its voyage tells you the Coast Guard found something significant enough to warrant a detention."

Perez said the U.S. Coast Guard has the authority to inspect and board vessels in U.S. ports.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"A lot of cruise ships are foreign-flagged. That doesn't change the Coast Guard's authority over them," he said.

In addition to a canceled vacation, many passengers worry about the price of additional airfare, accommodations and lost paid time off from work.

Perez said cruise passengers can file claims, but no class-action lawsuits are permitted.

The binding passenger ticket contract issued by all major cruise lines explicitly prohibits class-action lawsuits.

Under the universally enforced terms, passengers waive their right to join group litigation, according to the MSC USA Booking Conditions document.

"Cruise ship contracts prohibit class actions," Perez said. "So in a case like this ... they cannot do class actions to group themselves together and make it easier for the passenger to get relief," he said. 

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Several people took to online forums to discuss what happened.

"We have been on board the MSC Poesia since 28 September," said one Reddit user.

"During dinner, we noticed we had not left the harbor at the given time," the MSC passenger continued.

"Although we’re disappointed that the last part of our extended back-to-back cruise was canceled, we appreciate the compensation MSC has offered and the practical help they’re providing to get us home," the poster added.

"Must have been a heck of an error for [the] Coast Guard to keep them from sailing," another person commented. 

"I assume someone will spill the beans on what the problem was eventually."
